cards.explanation: The answer is that Job asks how a mortal can be righteous before God. Job takes Bildad's point and turns it into a question: “…how can a mortal be righteous before God?” (Job 9:2). He asks it about a mortal, any mortal. That's a heavy question, friends, and Job asks it plainly.

The answer is not once in a thousand times. Job says that person “…could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.” (Job 9:3). A thousand tries and not a single good answer. I once had a whole tray where not one cookie held its shape, and even that was a better record than this. Job is showing how far apart a mortal and God stand.

The answer is how mighty His power is. Job just called God “…mighty in strength.” (Job 9:4), and then he piles up the proof. Mountains move, the earth shakes and the sun is commanded not to shine (Job 9:5-7). Job says He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8). That's what Job wants everyone to see about Him.

The answer is True. Job says it right out: “He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south.” (Job 9:9). Those are star groups in the sky, and God made every one. Berry, one of my cookie cutter kids, was always at the window staring at the night sky. I think he would have loved that verse.

The answer is False. Job says, “Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him.” (Job 9:11). God could go right by, and Job says he wouldn't see Him or recognize Him. Job says God is that far beyond him.

The answer is that no one can stop Him. Job asks, “If He takes away, who can stop Him?” (Job 9:12). He asks it as a question, but he means that nobody can. Not a mountain, not a mortal, not a whole crowd of arguers. That's the weight of what Job is saying.

The answer is False. Job says, “God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him.” (Job 9:13). So he says God doesn't hold it back. This Rahab isn't the Rahab of Jericho. Job says her helpers cower, which tells you how Job pictures God's strength.

The answer is mercy. Job says, “For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy.” (Job 9:15). Even in the right, he sees himself begging. He calls God his Judge here. Mercy is the word Job lands on.

The answer is that God won't let him catch his breath. Job says, “He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness.” (Job 9:18). That's one hard picture, friends. It's like one wave after another with no gap between them. Job says there's no break.

The answer is his own mouth. Job says, “Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me; if I were blameless, it would declare me guilty.” (Job 9:20). So in his picture, even his own words would work against him. It's like walking into a meeting and tripping over your own sentence. Job says it would happen even if he were righteous.

The answer is True. Job says, “Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life.” (Job 9:21). He calls himself blameless in his own words. Back at the start of the book, he's described as “blameless and upright” (Job 1:1). Then he adds how much he despises his own life, which is a lot to carry.

The answer is the wicked. Job says, “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges.” (Job 9:24). That's what he sees when he looks around. It's Job's view of the world from deep inside his pain. The wicked are the ones holding it.

The answer is that his days are rushing by fast. Job says, “My days are swifter than a runner; they flee without seeing good.” (Job 9:25). A runner, boats of papyrus and an eagle swooping down are all fast things (Job 9:26). He's saying his days zip past. That's how it feels to him.

The answer is that he would still dread all his sufferings. Job says, “I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me.” (Job 9:28). Putting on a smile wouldn't change what he's carrying. A smile on the outside is just a smile, friends. Job says the dread stays.

The answer is False. Job says that even if he washed with snow and lye, “…then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me.” (Job 9:30-31). Scrubbing doesn't help in his picture. That's how stuck he feels.

The answer is mediator. Job says, “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both.” (Job 9:33). A mediator is someone who stands in the middle of two sides. Job says there's no one like that between him and God. That's the empty spot he points to.
The answer is False. Job says, “Then I would speak without fear of Him. But as it is, I am on my own.” (Job 9:35). The “then” is for after God's rod is removed. For now, he says he's on his own.

The answer is why God is prosecuting him. Job says, “I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why You prosecute me.” (Job 10:2). He wants a reason. I think anybody in pain would ask the same thing, friends. He asks it straight to God.

The answer is searching out his sin. Job asks if God's days are like a man's, “…that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin…” (Job 10:6). So this is what Job says God is doing to him. It's how Job sees it. Job is asking God to look at that.

The answer is True. Job says it right in his question to God: “…though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand?” (Job 10:7). So Job says God knows he isn't guilty. In the same breath, he says there's no deliverance from God's hand.
The answer is clay. Job says, “Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?” (Job 10:9). Clay is something hands shape. Job is reminding God of who made him.

The answer is True. Job says, “You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit.” (Job 10:12). Right after all the hard words, Job says this. He looks back and names God's care. I think it's a gentle moment in a heavy passage.

The answer is that he still cannot lift his head. Job says, “If I am guilty, woe to me! And even if I am righteous, I cannot lift my head.” (Job 10:15). So even in the righteous case, he says he can't lift his head. He adds that he is “…full of shame and aware of my affliction.” (Job 10:15). That's how low he feels.

The answer is His anger. Job says, “You produce new witnesses against me and multiply Your anger toward me.” (Job 10:17). That's how Job sees it. He adds that hardships assault him “…in wave after wave.” (Job 10:17). It's one thing after another.

The answer is False. Job says, “Are my days not few? Withdraw from me, that I may have a little comfort…” (Job 10:20). He asks God to pull back, not come closer. It sounds to me like a man asking for a little rest.

The answer is False. Job calls it “…a land of darkness and gloom…” and “…a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, where even the light is like darkness.” (Job 10:21-22). It's about as dark as he can put it. I think this part is heavy, friends.
